entities.summary: Gíallchad, the son of Ailill Olcháin, son of Sírna Sáeglach, was, according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition, the 37th High King of Ireland. Gíallchad took power after killing his predecessor, and the son of his grandfather's killer, Elim Olfínechta, in the battle of Comair Trí nUisce. He is said to have taken one out of every five men of Munster hostage. Gíallchad reigned for nine years, before being killed by Elim's son Art Imlech at Mag Muaide. The Lebor Gabála Érenn synchronises his reign with that of Phraortes of the Medes.

entities.name: Gíallchad
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gíallchad, son of Ailill Olcháin, son of Sírna Sáeglach, was, according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition, the 37th High King of Ireland. Gíallchad took power after killing his predecessor and, according to some accounts, avenged the killing of his grandfather's killer — a narrative of intergenerational vengeance that recurs throughout the legendary king-lists as a structural motif.

Gíallchad belongs to the deep mythological layer of the Irish High King tradition, compiled by monastic scholars in the 8th–10th centuries CE as part of the project of constructing a continuous pre-Christian Irish regal pedigree. His position as the 37th High King places him in the middle of the long sequence of legendary rulers that precede the historical period — a sequence designed to give Ireland's medieval dynasties the same depth of royal ancestry that biblical and classical genealogies provided.

The name Gíallchad contains the element 'gíall' (hostage/pledge), which may indicate a legendary role in the hostage-taking practices that were central to Irish political relationships. His story, like those of Lugaid Íardonn, Sírlám, and Fíachu Findoilches, follows the standard pattern of violent succession — kill, reign, be killed — that structures the entire pre-Christian segment of the High King lists. These figures served a primarily genealogical function for medieval Irish dynasties claiming descent from the ancient kings.
